Self-attention limits working memory capacity of transformer-based models

Arcs show where the current letter's attention goes (thickness = attention weight). The dashed tick marks the position N back, the one the task depends on.

Large language models get worse at the N-back task as N grows, much as people do. We trained the smallest transformer that can do the task, a single masked self-attention head with no feed-forward block, and found the same decline. Its attention gradually gathers onto the position N steps back, and the farther back that is, the more diffuse it stays. Total attention entropy rises with N as accuracy falls, which points to self-attention itself as the source of the capacity limit.

Background

A capacity limit with no obvious cause

Working memory is the ability to hold a few pieces of task-relevant information in mind and work with them. In people it is famously small, and the classic way to measure it is the N-back task: letters arrive one at a time, and you respond whenever the current letter matches the one shown N steps earlier. Accuracy falls steadily as N rises.

Earlier work from our group (Gong et al., 2024) gave GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 the same task and found the same pattern. That is surprising. Each sequence is only 24 letters, far inside the models' context windows, so running out of context cannot explain it. Something in how the model reads its context has to.

Cognitive psychology offers a candidate. Under executive attention theory (Engle, Kane and colleagues), working memory capacity is limited less by storage than by the attention needed to keep the right items active against interference from the rest. Transformers have an explicit attention mechanism. Our hypothesis is that self-attention plays the same role, and imposes the same kind of limit.

Setup

A transformer stripped down to attention

To isolate attention we removed everything else. The model embeds each letter, adds a learned position embedding, passes the sequence through one causally masked self-attention head, and maps each position straight to two outputs: m (match) or - (no match). There is no feed-forward network and no layer normalization, so any computation across positions has to happen inside the attention head.

TaskN-back, N = 1…6
Alphabetbcdfghjklnpqrstvwxyz
Sequence length24 letters
Matches per sequence8 of 24
Data per N800 train · 200 test
Model widthd = 512
TrainingAdam, lr 1e-4, batch 32, 10 epochs, cross-entropy at every position
Replicates50 models per N per architecture
Variantslayers L ∈ {1, 2}, heads H ∈ {1, 2, 4}
Result 1

The model reproduces the human-like decline

The single-head model's accuracy drops as N rises: from about 88% on 1-back to 84% on 3-back across 50 independently trained models each (Kruskal–Wallis H = 38.5, p < .001, ε² = 0.25). Extending to 6-back, the fall follows a roughly logarithmic curve that flattens out near 84%. Adding heads lifts accuracy above 94%, but most of those models still dip slightly as N grows.

Result 2

Attention learns to look N steps back

Watching the attention matrix over training shows how the model solves the task. At first every row is nearly uniform: each position spreads its attention evenly over everything before it. Over the epochs, weight collects on a single off-diagonal line, the line where position i attends to position i − N. Early positions get there first. Later positions have more letters behind them competing for attention, and their rows stay more spread out.

Result 3

More attention on the target, better answers

At each position, accuracy tracks how much attention lands on the letter N steps back. As training goes on, points climb up and to the right together. Coloring the same points by position shows the cost of distance into the sequence: later positions sit lower on both axes, because more preceding letters compete for the same attention.

Result 4

Attention spreads out as N grows

To measure how focused attention is, we sum the Shannon entropy of every row of the attention matrix. Each row is a probability distribution over the positions a letter can see, so a row that puts all its weight on one letter scores 0, and a row spread evenly over i letters scores ln i.

HN(A) = − Σi=124 Σj=1i Aij log Aij,    A = softmax(QKT / √dk)

Perfectly uniform attention gives ln 24! ≈ 54.8 nats; perfect focus gives 0. Across models, total entropy rises with N while accuracy falls. Our reading is that the model is less certain which earlier letter matters, so it hedges by spreading attention, and the hedge is what costs it accuracy.

Playground

Give the model your own sequence

This is the actual trained network, not a recording. Because it has no feed-forward block or normalization, its weights reduce exactly to a few small lookup tables, so the forward pass runs here in a few microseconds. Type letters from the model's alphabet, pick which task the model was trained on, and click any position to see where it looked.

Discussion

The same mechanism enables and limits

Self-attention is what makes the task solvable: without it no position could see an earlier letter. It is also where the limit comes from. Attention is a fixed budget that sums to one in every row, and finding the one relevant letter among more and more competitors gets harder the farther back it sits. That mirrors selective attention in the brain, which filters what gets processed and in doing so caps how much can be.

If capacity limits come from a trade-off between how much information is processed and how precisely, that trade-off can be designed around. We see this as a route toward architectures with larger working memory, and toward a formal account of why capacity limits appear in complex systems at all.

Scope. The model is deliberately minimal (one head, no feed-forward block, no normalization), so the comparison to pretrained LLMs is by analogy, not direct. Model size, data size, and other hyperparameters were not varied systematically, and the relationships in Results 3 and 4 are reported descriptively.
